title: To the End of the Earth
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to Finisterre and Muxía
author: CaminoPlus

spans.t: Every other Camino ends in Santiago. This one begins there.

Leave the Praza do Obradoiro with the cathedral at your back and the road runs west to the Atlantic. The Xunta de Galicia, the regional government, says Cape Finisterre (in Galician, Fisterra) is ~89 km from Santiago and the sanctuary of the Virxe da Barca at Muxía ~87 km. That is three to five walking days, depending on how you cut them and which source you ask. It is the shortest road in this series, and in its way the strangest: you walk away from the goal everyone else has walked towards.
The promise of this book is simple.

By the last page you will know what this road is, how to cut it into days, what the sea and the wind ask of you, what the official sources say about the certificates of the coast, and why the old custom of burning your boots at the cape is one to leave alone.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order: the Way in brief, whether it suits you, when to go, and what to do before you go. Then read the days, and the chapter on ways to split them, which matters more here than on most routes because the sources do not agree on the number of days.
If you are on the road tonight, go to your stage. If you are only dreaming, read "Is this Camino for you?" and "The inner Way".
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change, and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly. For those, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
It is also
not a Compostela book
. The Compostela, the certificate of the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago, belongs to the walk that arrives at the cathedral. This walk begins where that one ends.
Every distance carries a tilde,

, because it is approximate. The official sources give different figures for the same stage, and the book says so where it matters. Where something depends on the season (a closure, a fire warning, the state of the sea), it says
check before you go
, and means it.
A few words you will meet
Buen Camino
, "good Way", is what pilgrims and locals say as you pass. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a card stamped along the way; each stamp is a
sello
. A
ría
is a long sea inlet, and an
hórreo
a Galician granary on stone legs. The glossary at the end has the rest.
Pack lightly, bring something windproof, and be on the cape in time for the light.
Buen Camino.
Where it goes

The Xunta de Galicia describes the Fisterra and Muxía Way as a route that "originates in the city of Santiago" and has two goals: Cape Fisterra and the sanctuary of the Virxe da Barca in Muxía. It starts in the Praza do Obradoiro, crosses the Tambre at the bridge of Ponte Maceira, passes through Negreira and Olveiroa, and meets the sea at Cee and Corcubión. Fisterra is the first goal. Muxía lies to the north, on a peninsula of its own, and is the second.

The CaminoPlus catalog gives the road to Finisterre as ~90 km, and the sources keep close to it. The Xunta's four stages to the lighthouse add up to ~90 km, and its own text says ~89 km to Fisterra and ~87 km to Muxía. The Concello de Muxía, the town council, gives ~86.5 km from Santiago to the sanctuary, and the Concello de Fisterra's three stages add up to ~88 km. If you want both capes, the Xunta gives the whole road as ~118.8 km going to Fisterra first, and ~119.9 km going to Muxía first.
The Way that leaves Santiago
Every other route in this series is a way
to
Santiago. This is a way
from

it. The Concello de Fisterra calls it the only Camino whose goal is not Santiago but its origin. The Xunta writes that after kneeling before the apostle many pilgrims decide to see "this end of the world", and calls the route the most faithful realisation of the old pilgrims' cry
Ultreia
, "farther beyond", answered by
Et suseia
, "and higher".
What it feels like

The first two days are inland and green: oak groves, small rivers, stone bridges, hamlets, hórreos, gorse and pine and eucalyptus. The sea does not show itself until the third day, when, as the Xunta puts it, you first see Cape Fisterra from the Cruceiro da Armada, a viewpoint at ~247 m, "still far off". After that the road belongs to the Atlantic: the ría of Corcubión, the long beach of Langosteira, the lighthouse at the end of the cape, then the beaches and headlands on the way to Muxía.
Why it exists
The name Finisterre comes from the Latin
finis terrae

, "end of the earth", and in Roman times, as Wikipedia puts it, the cape was believed to be an end of the known world. The Concello de Fisterra says the idea of a pilgrimage towards the westernmost lands of Europe was already present in Celtic beliefs, bound up with the sun's daily journey. Turismo de Galicia, the regional tourism board, tells how the Roman general Decimus Junius Brutus came to believe that this was where the sun died at dusk. Wikipedia's account of that general's campaign, in 138 to 136 BC, takes him no further than southern Gallaecia, so treat the story as a legend, and a good one.

The Christian pilgrimage is well documented only from the Middle Ages. A heritage report of 2013 on a Xunta website, written in Galician (the translations here are the book's own), finds the first unmistakable reference to Fisterra as a long-distance pilgrimage place in the bequest of a canon of Santiago in 1283, which lists it with Rocamadour and Roncesvalles. Its oldest news of Muxía is from 1446, when Sebastian Ilsung, a pilgrim from Augsburg, came to see the stone boat. Wikipedia sums up the position honestly: the origin of the pilgrimage to Finisterre is not certain.

The report adds something worth knowing before you leave. Most of the medieval accounts it quotes show travellers who were passive (they went because they had been told in Santiago that one must), curious (to see the end of the world) and even offhand. Domenico Laffi, writing in 1673, treated the trip as a whim. You do not have to be sure why you are going.
A road with its own rules

This is not a Compostela route. In the Pilgrim's Office's wording, the final stage of the walk that earns the Compostela must include the last stretch leading into the cathedral, and this walk leaves the cathedral behind. The Office's pages read for this book say nothing about Fisterra or Muxía. The certificates of the coast, the Fisterrana and the Muxiana, are another matter, and the chapter on arriving says where the official sources place them.
How hard is it?

The Xunta rates the whole road of medium difficulty, in both directions. It rates the single stages less evenly. Santiago to Negreira (~20.9 km) and Corcubión to Fisterra (~14.2 km) are marked high, and so is the day from Fisterra to Muxía (~28.7 km). The long day, Negreira to Olveiroa (~34.3 km, estimated at ~7 h 45 min), is marked only medium. Spain's official tourism website takes the opposite view and calls the route five comfortable stages with no significant gradients.

Both can be true. This is not mountain walking. The high points the Xunta's text names are modest: Mount Aro at ~556 m on the long second day, the Cruceiro da Armada at ~247 m, and As Aferroas at ~289 m before Muxía. But the climbs come in short, steep pitches, and the Xunta describes the stage from Corcubión to Fisterra as short but of a high level of difficulty. Treat a figure as a guide, and your own legs as the answer.
Who it suits

items.t: Anyone who has just arrived in Santiago and is not ready to stop.
That is the oldest reason for this road, and a good one.
A first long walk.
Five days or fewer is a manageable commitment, and you can shorten it, as a later chapter shows.
Walkers who want the sea.
This road ends on the Atlantic, at two capes.
Anyone who walks for reasons beyond a certificate.
There is no Compostela at the end of this road, so the walk has to be worth it for its own sake. For many people that is exactly its appeal.

spans.t: Who might choose another

items.t: If you need the Compostela.
It is issued for a walk that arrives at the cathedral, and this one leaves it. If the certificate matters to you, choose a route that ends in Santiago and read the rule at the Pilgrim's Office.
If a day of ~34 km is out of reach.
It can be split, and the chapter on ways to split the days shows how, but splitting depends on where you can stay, which is a question for the app and the phone.
If you want a landscape of villages all day.
The Xunta's text describes small hamlets, a mix of asphalt and rural roads, and long stretches of country. The coast is exposed. Pack for wind and rain, and carry food and water for the long day.
If heights or steep drops trouble you.
The cape has cliffs over the Atlantic.

spans.t: How it compares

The Camino Inglés, another short route in this series, is ~113 km from Ferrol and ends in Santiago. The road to Finisterre is shorter and goes the other way. If you have five days and a wish to see the Atlantic, choose this one. If you have six days and a wish to arrive at the cathedral, choose that one. The road to the sea is not a lesser Camino. It is the walk of someone who already knows what the cathedral looks like.
The weather, in patterns

Galicia is green because it is wet. No official coastal climate table was read for this book, so these figures are for Santiago, where the road begins. Wikipedia gives them from the Spanish state weather agency, AEMET, for 1991 to 2020. The sea will be windier than the city, and no table here says by how much.

items.t: Winter.
In January the average daily high in Santiago is ~12 °C and the low ~5 °C. The wettest months are October (~214 mm of rain), January (~196 mm), November (~194 mm) and December (~184 mm).
Spring.
April averages a high of ~17 °C and ~130 mm of rain, May ~20 °C and ~109 mm. The rain eases month by month.
Summer.
July is the driest month (~31 mm), with an average high of ~25 °C and a low of ~14 °C. June (~44 mm) and August (~45 mm) are nearly as dry. Hot spells can run well above the average.
Autumn.
September is mild (~23 °C by day, ~89 mm), and the rain returns hard in October.

spans.t: The CaminoPlus route guide in the app suggests April to October for this road. That fits the table: it is the dry half of the year, and the half with the long evenings.

For the coast itself, ask the people who watch it. AEMET publishes a forecast for the municipality of Fisterra, the Galician weather service MeteoGalicia forecasts for all of Galicia, and the Concello de Fisterra's website keeps pages for the weather and the tides. Read them the evening before, and again at breakfast.
Daylight, and the light you came for

The best moment of this walk is at a fixed time of day, so light matters here more than on a road that ends in a town square. These are the book's own figures, calculated from a standard solar formula for the cape, in local clock time. They are approximate, cloud decides whether you see anything, and you should check them against a sun table before you plan.

items.t: Late December: sunrise ~09:05, sunset ~18:05, about ~9 hours of daylight.
Mid-November: sunset ~18:15.
Late March: sunset ~19:50.
Mid-April: sunset ~21:20.
Late June: sunrise ~07:00, sunset ~22:20, about ~15 hours of daylight.
Late September: sunset ~20:40.
Mid-October: sunset ~19:55.

spans.t: In summer you can walk a long day and still reach the lighthouse for sunset. In winter, a late start puts you on the cliff road in the dusk. Plan to arrive with at least an hour of light, and carry a head torch.
Crowds and quiet

No count of pilgrims on this road was found in a source that could be checked. The Pilgrim's Office's statistics page is built by script and could not be read, and its other pages do not mention this walk. In winter the days are short, the weather is rough, and some places are shut for the season, which is a question for the app and a phone call, not for this book.
The Holy Year.

A Jacobean Holy Year falls when 25 July is a Sunday, and the next is 2027. The Pilgrim's Office says that 272,703 pilgrims qualified for the Compostela in the Holy Year of 2010, against 1,245 who arrived in 1985, and it warns that in times of great influx it cannot promise to issue the Compostela on the day you ask. Santiago will be busy in 2027. Whether the road to the coast will be busier too is not something any source read for this book says.
Check before you go

Fire, closures, a diversion, the state of the sea: these change from year to year and from day to day. Check the Xunta's pages for the route, the app and the weather services above, and ask locally on the way.
Your credencial
The
credencial
is the pilgrim's passport: a folded card with boxes for the stamps, or
sellos

, that you collect on the way. The Pilgrim's Office says the stamps are normally collected where pilgrims sleep, but can also be had in parish churches, monasteries, cathedrals, hotels, town halls and other places. It also says where to get an official card: from the confraternities of St James and from authorised associations, in Spain and abroad.

On this road the credencial matters for one reason. The Concello de Fisterra says the route you have walked is shown by the credencial, with the stamps or signatures of parishes, hostels and other places on the road. The pages read for this book do not say how many stamps are expected, or whether the stamps from your walk to Santiago count. Ask where you plan to collect the certificate, and carry a card with room on it. If you have just walked to Santiago, check how many boxes are left. A stamp from Santiago on the morning you leave is a good first one.
Getting there, and getting back
The road starts in the Praza do Obradoiro, in front of the cathedral, as the Xunta says. The airport, Santiago-Rosalía de Castro, is ~12 km east of the city, according to Wikipedia.

Getting back needs thought. Fisterra and Muxía are small towns, and this book names no timetables, because they change. The Xunta runs a public transport website, bus.gal, where it says passengers can look up the times of its bus lines, and an older item in its news archive announces a line between Santiago, Cee and Fisterra. No source read for this book gives a current timetable for Fisterra or Muxía. Check before you leave Santiago, ask at your hostel or the tourist office the evening before you travel, and use the app. Do not plan your flight home for the afternoon of your last walking day.
Training and packing

The Xunta's advice for every Camino applies: do not set off untrained. Take long walks in the weeks before you go, lengthen them gradually, and draw up a plan of stages that matches your fitness. With a longest day of ~34 km, a practice walk of ~20 km with your loaded pack, and two long days in a row, are a sensible test.

Keep the pack light. The Xunta says a correctly packed rucksack should not exceed 10 kg, with padded straps to prevent chafing. Its basics are a water bottle, footwear for the evening, high-protection sunscreen, a small first-aid kit, a phone with a charger, and your documents. It adds that a waterproof garment belongs in the pack at any time of year, and a cap is useful all year, for sun and for cold. The coast adds three things:

items.t: A windproof layer
, and a warm one for the cape, where the wind off the sea cools you fast, especially at dusk.
A head torch
, because the way down from the lighthouse can be after dark.
A bag for your boots, if you want to carry them home.
A later chapter says why.

spans.t: Shoes and feet

The Xunta is clear that footwear must be comfortable and already broken in, because new stiff shoes will hurt you. It recommends seamless socks, dry feet, and washing and drying socks at every stop. For anything that worries you, see a pharmacist or a doctor, and do it early.
Money and language
The Xunta advises carrying your documents and cards rather than a lot of cash. The villages on this road are small, so carry a little cash for places that do not take cards.

Galicia has two official languages, Galician and Spanish. The Xunta's texts use the Galician forms of names, and so do the town councils' pages: Fisterra for Finisterre, Muxía for Mugía. You will also meet Galician words such as
rúa
(street),
praza
(square),
ponte
(bridge),
camiño
(path, way) and
hórreo
(the granary on stone legs). This book uses the Galician names and gives the Spanish ones where they help.

chapters.title: The inland days: Santiago to Olveiroa

spans.t: The character of these days

The first two days go west through country that has changed little in its outline: oak groves, stone bridges over the Sarela and the Tambre, hamlets of granaries and small fields. There is no sea, and the first day begins with a city to leave behind. The second is the long one.

The lengths in this book follow the Xunta's stage pages. Other sources differ by a kilometre or two. The Concello de Fisterra has the first two stages at ~22 km and ~33 km, Spain's official tourism website at ~20 km and ~34 km, and one travel agency's route page at ~20.6 km, with the second day ending at a town just over ~1 km off the route. Treat each figure as a good guide, not a measurement.
Day 1: Santiago to Negreira (~21 km)

The Xunta rates this stage high and estimates ~4 h 20 min. It starts as every Camino ends: in the Praza do Obradoiro. You leave by the line of the vanished Porta do Peregrino, the Pilgrim's Gate, also called the Porta da Trindade, down the Costa do Cristo and along the Rúa das Hortas, past the church of San Frutuoso. A document of 1536, according to a Xunta heritage report, already names this street as the way to Fisterra. Then comes the oak grove of San Lourenzo, with oaks the Xunta calls centenarian, and the countryside that the poet Rosalía de Castro wrote about in
Follas novas

The way drops to the River Sarela, where the Xunta notes the ruins of the tanneries on the bank: Santiago had a thriving leather trade until the last thirty years of the 19th century. After that a stony path climbs to the first houses of Sarela de Abaixo. The same heritage report says that from the top of this steep final climb you see the towers of the cathedral for the last time. Stop and look: it is your last sight of the city.

Then the road is country: Villestro, Roxos, Alto do Vento, a medieval bridge with a rounded arch at Augapesada, and a hard climb to the top of the Mar de Ovellas, with views over the valley of A Maía. The first ~8.9 km, to Alto do Vento, are rated medium to high by the Xunta, which fits its high rating for the whole day.

The day's great sight is the bridge at Ponte Maceira over the Tambre, which the Xunta calls the most outstanding bridge of this Camino. The heritage report says it was built at some point in the 15th century, and that people crossed by ferry at about the same spot before that. Spain's official tourism website adds that the village has an old mill, a dam, the chapel of San Blas and a 19th-century manor house, and calls it one of the most beautiful villages in Spain. Cross it slowly.

Negreira comes soon after. The Xunta calls it the largest town, with over 2,000 inhabitants, that the pilgrim crosses before reaching the coast. At the entrance, the coat of arms of the Pazo de A Chancela shows a bridge: the one, according to Book III of the Codex Calixtinus, that was destroyed to stop the soldiers pursuing the disciples of St James. Hemingway mentions the town in
For Whom the Bell Tolls
, a fact the Xunta and Spain's tourism website both note. You pass the chapel of San Mauro and the Pazo do Cotón on the way through.
Go gently on the first day. It has a hard climb in it, and tomorrow is long.
Day 2: Negreira to Olveiroa (~34 km)

This is the longest stage of the road. The Xunta rates it medium and estimates ~7 h 45 min. Spain's official tourism website agrees that it is the longest and calls the slopes gentle. It is not a day to start late.

Several stretches, the Xunta says, follow the old Camiño Real to Fisterra, and the place names show it: Camiño Real, Portocamiño. You cross the River Barcala on leaving Negreira and climb to the hamlet of Negreiroa, which the Xunta calls the original nucleus of Negreira. Then the road is countryside: gorse, cornfields, pine and eucalyptus, hórreos (the Xunta singles out those of As Maroñas) and Romanesque churches, such as that of Santa Mariña. After O Cornado you leave the municipality of Negreira for the region of Xallas.

Mount Aro, at ~556 m according to the Xunta, is the high point named in its text: a viewpoint over the Terra de Xallas, a country the Xunta says is known for basketry and for its women's straw hats. After the viewpoint of Corzón and the village of Mollón you reach the bridge over the River Xallas, the boundary between the municipalities of Mazaricos and Dumbría. Then A Ponte Olveira and the centre of Olveiroa, where the stage ends.

The heritage report lists the stops that were obligatory on the old royal road to Corcubión and Fisterra, and they are the places you pass: Augapesada, Ponte Maceira, As Maroñas, Ponte Olveira, Olveiroa. It also names travellers who left an account of this ground, such as Erich Lassota in the 1580s and Domenico Laffi in 1673.

Carry food and water for this day, and eat before you are hungry. Whether a place along the way is open is a question for the app and the phone. If the day is too long for you, the chapter on variants shows other ways to cut it.

chapters.title: To the sea: Olveiroa to Fisterra

spans.t: The character of these days

The third day brings the sea into view, and the fourth puts you beside it. The two days together are shorter than the long day behind you: ~20.7 km and ~14.2 km by the Xunta's figures, which add up to ~34.9 km. The Concello de Fisterra, whose own page counts three stages to the cape, runs the whole stretch from Olveiroa to Fisterra as one stage of ~33 km. This book follows the Xunta and takes it in two, because the second half is the part to walk slowly.
The sources agree on the shape and differ on the numbers. Spain's official tourism website has ~20 km and ~14 km, and one travel agency's page, which ends its third day at Cee, has ~21 km and ~16 km.
Day 3: Olveiroa to Corcubión (~21 km)

The Xunta rates this stage medium to high and estimates ~4 h 25 min. You leave Olveiroa with the Xallas flowing below you, hemmed in by trees, cross the River Hospital, pass through O Logoso and reach the hamlet of Hospital. It once had a modest pilgrims' hospital, which has gone. Shortly after, at a roundabout, the road forks. This is the fork of the ways to Fisterra and to Muxía, in the Xunta's words. If you take the Fisterra branch you walk to the sea first, and this chapter follows it. The ways to take the other branch are in the chapter on variants.

After the fork the road climbs towards the sanctuary of Nosa Señora das Neves, Mount Ousado and the hermitage of San Pedro Mártir, in the parish of A Pereiriña. Then, on the heights of the Cruceiro da Armada, at ~247 m, the Xunta says you can see Cape Fisterra for the first time, still far off. Spend a minute there. It is the first sight of where you are going.

A steep descent over the ría of Corcubión brings you to Cee. The Xunta calls it the first town of the region that the pilgrim reaches, and the largest municipality on the Costa da Morte, with notable commercial activity. Corcubión is next door. Its old quarter has been declared a historic-artistic complex, and the Xunta points to the church of San Marcos, in the Maritime Gothic style, from the end of the 15th century. It holds an image of the patron of the town that was made in northern Italy in the late 15th or early 16th century.

The heritage report calls Corcubión the most important town and port of that stretch of coast, and says the royal road from Santiago ran to it. From Corcubión to Fisterra, then an insignificant port in the report's words, there seems to have been no royal road at all.
Day 4: Corcubión to Fisterra (~14 km)

The Xunta calls this a short stage with a high level of difficulty, ending at the lighthouse, and estimates ~3 h. It starts with a steep climb from the Campo do Rollo in Corcubión to the Campo de San Roque and the hamlet of O Vilar, passes through A Amarela and Estorde, and runs along stretches of the old Camiño Real at Sardiñeiro.

Then the coast takes over. The Xunta says that you cross a region with one of the most beautiful shorelines of the Iberian Peninsula: wide, calm sands cushioning a rocky shore, and a very rough sea that has left hundreds of stories and legends of shipwrecks. You skirt the Cala do Talón, pass Calcova and come to the long beach of Langosteira, with the town of Fisterra rising in the distance like an island. The marked path runs between the dunes, and the Xunta notes that many pilgrims choose to finish the stage on the beach. If you do, look at the tide first. The Concello de Fisterra publishes a tide page on its website.

Langosteira has a place in the old customs. The Concello's page on the old rites says that the bath of purification was taken on this beach, two kilometres before the village, so that the pilgrim shook off the dust of the whole road and began the last approach clean. Spain's official tourism website calls the beach a good place for a swim, weather permitting. The sea here is rough, and the chapter on safety says what that means. Do not decide it on a whim.

You enter Fisterra by the district of San Roque, pass the cruceiro of Baixar, and follow the Rúa Santa Catarina and the Rúa Real. Fisterra is an old port and fishing town, according to Wikipedia, and the Xunta says the road up to the lighthouse passes the church of Santa María das Areas, where the Santo Cristo of Fisterra is kept. The next chapter takes you up.
You may arrive with time to spare, because this is the short day. That is the point. The best light of the walk is at the end of it, and the next chapter says how to keep the evening for it.

chapters.title: At the cape: sunset, sea and boots

spans.t: The lighthouse and the zero

The Xunta ends its stage at the lighthouse and calls the tip of the cape kilometre zero of the Way of St James. The lighthouse was built in 1853, according to Spanish Wikipedia, after a decision taken in 1843. It is an octagonal granite tower, ~17 m high, on a promontory ~120 m above the sea, with a fog siren from 1888, a hint that fog is part of the cape's weather. Wikipedia's pictures of the cape show a bronze sculpture of a pilgrim's boot.
Why it was the end of the earth

Finisterre is not the westernmost point of Spain or of Europe, and the sources say so. Wikipedia notes that Cape Touriñán, to the north, is ~124 m farther west, and that Cabo da Roca in Portugal lies ~16.5 km farther west than Finisterre. What made it the end of the earth was its look and its legend. Turismo de Galicia says that, according to legend, the Phoenicians raised an altar to the sun there, the Ara Solis, and that the Roman general Brutus took it for the place where the sun died at dusk. It also says that pilgrims who went on from Santiago followed the route the Milky Way marked out overhead, until they could go no further.

The Costa da Morte, the Coast of Death, is named for its shipwrecks. Wikipedia says the name first appeared in a newspaper article of 1904, after a run of wrecks. It mentions the loss of the torpedo cruiser HMS Serpent in 1890, with 173 of its 176 crew, and the sinking of the oil tanker Prestige in 2002, one of the worst oil spills in history. A local legend, Wikipedia adds, says that the wind here creates wild nightmares.
The sunset

The Concello de Fisterra's page on the old rites names two. The first is the bath of purification, at Langosteira. The second is to watch the sunset, which the Concello describes as the death of the sun in the sea and its resurrection the next day, like the pilgrim's resurrection in the daily walking. Turismo de Galicia says it is not every day that you get to see the sun go down at world's end.

Plan for it, and do not make it a test. The chapter on when to go gives the times, from ~18:05 at midwinter to ~22:20 at midsummer, and they are approximate. Cloud may take the show away, and the walk was never for the show alone. If you can, give the cape a whole evening, not an hour:

items.t: Go up with time to spare
, at least an hour before sunset, and carry a warm layer.
Know your way back before the light goes.
Carry a head torch and use it on the road.
Stay on the paths and behind the fences.
The lighthouse stands on a cliff, and the wind is strong. Never climb on wet rock to improve a photograph.
Stay for the last light.
The sky changes for a while after the sun has gone.

spans.t: The boots
Many pilgrims have taken up the custom of burning their boots or their clothes at the cape, as a way of leaving the old road behind. This book does not encourage it, and the town asks you not to.

The Concello's own page on the old rites does not mention burning at all. In October 2022 the news site Galicia Press quoted the Concello, which called burning a "false ritual" that turns a natural place into something like a dump and can even start forest fires. The same report said the town was launching a campaign,
Buen Camino, mejor final
("A good Way, a better ending"), with a container at the zero kilometre for boots and belongings, to be handled in a clean and sustainable way.

In June 2024 the newspaper El Debate reported that the burning had been stamped out in 2022, and that a new habit had grown in its place: tying clothes and other objects to the fence at the lighthouse. According to the paper, the council had put notices in the hostels, appealed to people's civic sense, and put the local authorities to fining anyone caught leaving things. It judged these measures insufficient, and noted that in the strong wind many of the objects end up in the sea. The pilgrim news site Vive Camino adds that fires from bonfires have happened in recent years, and that burning some items releases toxic fumes.

This book could not read the text of any local rule, so it gives no legal wording and no figure for a fine. It says only what these sources say. The sense of it is plain: do not light a fire at the cape, and do not leave things behind.
There are quieter ways to do what the fire was meant to do:

items.t: Carry the boots home.
That is what the bag in your pack is for.
If you must part with them,
ask the tourist office or your hostel what the town asks pilgrims to do, and use the container if it is still there.
Keep the ritual and drop the flame.
Write down what you are leaving behind and keep the paper in your pocket. Read it again in a month.

spans.t: The old rites the town names are the bath and the sunset. Those are enough.

chapters.title: The last day: Fisterra to Muxía

spans.t: The character of the day

The Xunta rates this stage high, gives it ~28.7 km and estimates ~7 h 15 min. It is the longest day since Negreira. The sources differ: ~32 km in the Xunta's figures for the same road walked the other way, ~29 km on Spain's official tourism website, ~31 km on one travel agency's page. Treat it as ~29 to ~31 km, and leave the whole day for it.
The day is mostly the sea: beaches, pinewoods, narrow quiet roads and a last climb. It ends at the sanctuary of Muxía, beside the water.
From Fisterra to Lires

Leaving Fisterra can be confusing, the Xunta warns, because yellow arrows point in opposite directions for pilgrims going to Muxía and those arriving from it, so keep a map or the app open at the start. You go back to Langosteira beach and, at the cruceiro of Baixar, take the way to the parish of San Martiño de Duio. The Xunta says the church may refer to a vanished Roman city, Dugium, which Book III of the Codex Calixtinus mentions. The Concello de Fisterra gives the old story as ancient testimonies tell it: a pagan city, Dugium (today Duio), through which the remains of the apostle passed on their way to burial at the edge of the West. The disciples asked leave of the queen of the region, Lupa, who sent them to the governor of Dugium. He ordered an ambush to kill them, but they discovered the plan and escaped.

The path runs past hamlets, woods and wheat fields, close to the sea. It comes to the sands of the beach of O Rostro among the pines, runs beside the beach, and climbs to the rural village of Padrís before the woods that lead to Lires. The first part, from Fisterra to Castrexe, is ~8.6 km and rated medium. The Xunta's text treats Lires as the end of the first part of the day, which makes it the natural place to break it if you need to. It stands on a ría that the Xunta says is rich in bird life, with the Romanesque churches of Frixe and Morquintián nearby. Whether you can stay there is a matter for the app and the phone.
From Lires to Muxía

After Lires you cross the River Castro, on a bridge that the Xunta says was inaugurated in 2011 and made the ford easier for pilgrims. Then come Vaosilveiro, Frixe and Morquintián, with stretches of asphalt and country road, and the last real effort of the day: the climb to As Aferroas, at ~289 m, and to Mount Facho de Lourido, which the Xunta calls an old lookout where local people lit bonfires to warn of danger on this coast. Then you skirt the beach of Lourido and enter Muxía by the Rúa Campo das Pinas.

The Xunta notes two things on the way into town. One is the tourist office, where you can obtain the Muxiana, the end-of-Camino certificate. The other is the Camiño da Pel, "the Way of the Skin", a path round Mount Corpiño named for a fountain that has disappeared. The Concello de Muxía says pilgrims and the sick washed there before entering the sanctuary, to avoid being infected with leprosy. The Xunta reads the name as a symbol of purification and respect. At the foot of the hill stands the church of Santa María de Muxía, Maritime Gothic, from the second half of the 14th century.
The sanctuary of the Virxe da Barca

Beyond the town, beside the sea, stands the sanctuary of the Virxe da Barca, the Virgin of the Boat, a Baroque church of the 18th century according to the Xunta. The legend, which the Concello de Muxía and Turismo de Galicia both tell, is that the Virgin Mary arrived here in a boat of stone to give courage to the apostle James in his preaching. The stones round the church are the remains of the boat. The Pedra de Abalar, the swaying stone, is a granite mass of ~70 tons that tradition identifies with the hull, and which Turismo de Galicia says now swings only intermittently because of a fracture. The Pedra do Temón is the helm. The Pedra dos Cadrís is shaped like a kidney, and tradition says you must pass under it nine times to be healed. The Pedra dos Namorados is the stone of the lovers.

The tradition is old. The heritage report quotes Sebastian Ilsung of Augsburg, who in 1446 called the stone boat the greatest of the miracles he had seen on his journey, and who adds that he saw the stone being moved.

The sanctuary has burnt and been rebuilt. On Christmas Day 2013 a fire, which Wikipedia says was caused by lightning, destroyed the roof and the altarpiece and left only the outer walls and a few furnishings standing, the Concello says. The church has been rebuilt several times, it adds, the last in 2015, and the number of visitors has risen since the fire. A great pilgrimage to the Virxe da Barca takes place every September, which the Concello says is recognised as being of national tourist interest.
Close by stands
A Ferida
, "The Wound", a sculpture by Alberto Bañuelos-Fournier made in tribute to the volunteers who fought the oil of the Prestige in 2002, as Turismo de Galicia notes.
The last of the light

Mount Corpiño, which the Concello de Muxía's pages put at ~67 to ~68 m, has a stone path to the top. The Concello says the view from it takes in the town, the sunset, the ría and the headland of Cape Vilán across the water. If you reach Muxía on a clear evening, that is the place to be. Take care on wet rock, here as at the other cape. The stones of the sanctuary are by the sea, and the sea is not tame.

chapters.title: Variants, and ways to split the days

spans.t: How many days? The sources differ
No two sources cut this road the same way, and the CaminoPlus catalog gives no stage count for it. Here is what each says.

items.t: The Concello de Fisterra
counts three stages to the cape: Santiago to Negreira (~22 km), Negreira to Olveiroa (~33 km) and Olveiroa to Fisterra (~33 km). That is ~88 km, and Muxía would be a fourth day.
The Xunta de Galicia

gives four stages to the lighthouse, Santiago to Negreira (~20.9 km), Negreira to Olveiroa (~34.3 km), Olveiroa to Corcubión (~20.7 km) and Corcubión to Fisterra (~14.2 km), and a fifth to Muxía (~28.7 km). Its own introduction speaks of pilgrims walking at least four or five days more after Santiago.
Spain's official tourism website
has five stages with the same towns, at ~20, ~34, ~20, ~14 and ~29 km.
One travel agency's route page
also has five, but cuts them differently: ~20.6 km to Negreira, ~31 km to a town just over ~1 km off the route, ~21 km to Cee, ~16 km to Fisterra and ~31 km to Muxía.

spans.t: So the honest answer is: three days to Fisterra and one to Muxía if you walk fast, five if you follow the Xunta, and more if you want to go slowly. This book follows the Xunta's five.
Plans that fit
These are sums of the sources' figures, which the book has added up, so they are approximate and carry the sources' differences.

items.t: Four days, both capes.
The Concello's three stages and the Xunta's last. It means two days of ~33 km in a row, then ~29 km. Only for the very fit and well prepared.
Five days, both capes.
The Xunta's plan, and the one in the chapters above: ~21, ~34, ~21, ~14, ~29 km. The long second day is the one to think about.
Six or seven days.

Split the long second day and the last day. For the second, the Xunta's own list of waypoints names O Cornado, Santa Mariña and Lago, and the travel agency above breaks it at a town just off the route. For the last, Lires is the natural break.
A rest day.
Fisterra and Muxía are both good places for one. Give one of them an evening and a morning.

spans.t: Whether you can sleep where you want to is a question for the app and the phone. Which places have a hostel changes from season to season, so this book names none.
Fisterra first, or Muxía first
At the roundabout after Hospital, the road forks. The Xunta says this is the fork of the ways to Fisterra and Muxía. You have a choice.
To Fisterra first, then Muxía.
This is the book's route: the sea at Cee, the cape, then the day along the coast to Muxía.
To Muxía first.

From Olveiroa the Xunta gives a direct stage of ~32.7 km, rated high and estimated at ~8 h 15 min. It goes by Dumbría, the municipal capital, and San Martiño de Ozón, with asphalt and country roads alternating. Near the end the road passes the Romanesque church of San Xulián de Moraime, close to the sea, and arrives at the sanctuary. Santiago to Muxía by this way is ~87 km, says the Xunta, and ~86.5 km, medium to high and about ~16 hours "more or less", says the Concello de Muxía. That is a three-day walk: the Xunta's first two stages and this one add up to ~87.9 km. From Muxía the Xunta then gives ~32 km, rated medium to high, to Fisterra. The whole road in this order is ~119.9 km.

Which end do you want to finish at? In one order you end at the cape and its lighthouse, in the other at the sanctuary and its stones. The Xunta publishes both. Choose by the ending you want, and by the light you want to see it in.
Check before you go
Waymarks, diversions and the state of the paths change. Before you set out, check the Xunta's pages for the stage you are about to walk, and the app.
Albergue life
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: a dormitory with bunk beds, a shared bathroom and often a place to wash your clothes. You show your credencial at the door and the host, the
hospitalero

, stamps it and tells you the house rules. The Xunta publishes a network of public hostels on its Camino portal, and the Concello de Fisterra refers to the municipal pilgrims' hostel in its town. Which places on this road have a hostel, and which are open this month, changes with the season, so this book lists none. The Xunta's stage pages also list hotels, guesthouses and rural lodgings. Use the app and the phone, and call ahead in the busy months.
The etiquette of a dormitory is short and kind.

items.t: Arrive, claim a bed, shower, wash and hang out your clothes. The evening is for resting.
Keep your voice low after the lights go out, and pack your rucksack in the hall, not in the dark by your bed.
Use a head torch, not the main light. Silence your phone.
Keep your pack and shoes off the bed.
Earplugs are a small comfort that goes a long way. If you are the one who snores, apologise at breakfast.

spans.t: Bedbugs can turn up in any shared bed. Look at the seams of the mattress before you lie down, keep your pack off the bed, and if you are bitten tell the host and wash and dry everything hot. If you are ill, tired or sleeping badly, take a private room. A good night is part of the walk.
Eating
Many places along a Camino offer a
menú del peregrino
, a set meal for pilgrims. Ask what it includes before you sit down. For the long days, carry food: the stretch from Negreira to Olveiroa, the Xunta's longest, runs through country.

The sea shapes the table here, and the official sources say what to look for. Turismo de Galicia sends you to Fisterra's harbour first, to watch the fishing boats and, if you like, to eat razor clams or other local seafood. Spain's official tourism website names the fish and shellfish stews called
caldeiradas
empanadas
, local beef,
polbo á feira
(Galician octopus) and the
tarta de Santiago
, the Santiago tart. You need not eat all of it. Pick one local thing a day, and eat it without a screen.
Fill your bottle whenever you can. The Xunta's health advice is to drink about two litres of water a day, and never to go beyond ~15 km without drinking.
Resting
A short road is easy to treat as a sprint. Do not. A day of rest is part of the walk, and this road has two natural places for one.
Fisterra
is the first. Give the cape an evening, and the town a morning. The harbour, the church of Santa María das Areas and its Santo Cristo, the beach of Langosteira: all are worth a slow hour.
Muxía
is the second. The sanctuary, the stones, Mount Corpiño at dusk and the fishing harbour make it a good place to stay an extra night and let the walk settle before you go back to Santiago.
On the road, listen to your body before your plan. If a pain grows instead of fading, stop, rest, and let a doctor look at it. You are not walking to prove anything.
This chapter is plain on purpose. Nothing here is a reason to be afraid of this road. It is a list of the things worth taking seriously on a short, exposed one.
Feet and legs

Your feet decide how the walk goes. Stop at the first hot spot and dress it before it becomes a blister. The Xunta's advice is to keep feet clean and dry, change damp socks, and never start with new shoes. Rest a few minutes each hour, take your pack off, and eat and drink before you are hungry or thirsty. If you feel a sharp or growing pain in a knee, a shin or the top of a foot, stop: a day lost to rest is better than a week lost to an injury. For anything that worries you, see a doctor or a pharmacist.
The exposed coast
The last three days are on the edge of the Atlantic. The Xunta describes a very rough sea off this shore, with hundreds of stories of shipwrecks. Plan for wind even on a fine day.

items.t: At the cape and at Muxía,
stay on the paths and behind the fences. The lighthouse stands ~120 m above the sea. Do not step onto wet rock for a photograph, at either place. The stones of the sanctuary are beside the water.
In the sea,

be careful. Spain's official tourism website calls Langosteira a good place for a swim, weather permitting. Weather permitting is the point. Swim only where and when it is clearly safe, never alone, never at dusk, never in rough water. If a flag, a sign or a local says no, the answer is no.
On the beach,
look at the tide before you choose it over the path in the dunes. The Concello de Fisterra publishes a tide page.
In fog,
slow down and keep to the marked way.

spans.t: Rain, cold and sun

The Xunta advises a waterproof garment on the Way at any time of year, and a cap against both sun and cold. Wet clothes cool you fast, even in mild weather. Carry a waterproof jacket, keep one dry layer in a bag that cannot get wet, and add a windproof layer for the cape. If you begin to shiver, stop somewhere warm before you try to go on. Do not start a long day in the dark; the chapter on when to go has the daylight figures. On a bright day, wear sunscreen and a hat, as the Xunta says.
Roads, paths and fires

Most of the way is on paths and quiet roads. The Xunta describes stretches where asphalt and country roads alternate, and narrow quiet roads on the way to Muxía. Where you must walk on a road, face the oncoming traffic, keep to the edge and wear something bright. Never walk on a road in the dark.

Do not light fires, at the cape or anywhere else on the road. The Concello de Fisterra says burning has started forest fires, and the wind on the cape is strong. In a dry summer, obey any fire warning you see.
When to stop

Tell someone where you will sleep each night, keep your phone charged and your map offline, and know the name of the last village you passed. If you are tired, ill or frightened by the weather, stop. The road will be there tomorrow, and so will the sea.
In an emergency in Spain, call 112,
the European emergency number.

People walk to the sea for many reasons, and they do not have to be yours. Some walk out of faith: the road begins at the cathedral of St James and ends at two places of old devotion, the Santo Cristo of Fisterra and the Virgin of the Boat at Muxía. Some walk for sport, or for a rest from work, or because the cathedral was not quite the end of something. Some walk out of grief, or at a turning point. Some are simply curious what a headland at the edge of Europe looks like at dusk. All are welcome on the road, and none needs to defend the reason.
After the cathedral

Every other Camino ends in Santiago. This one starts there. It is a different kind of walking: not towards an arrival but away from one. The Xunta calls it the most faithful realisation of the pilgrims' old cry,
Ultreia
, "farther beyond".

There is a long human record of how pilgrims went. The Xunta's heritage report says that most of the accounts it quotes from medieval travellers show people who were passive, curious and even offhand: they went because they had been told in Santiago that one had to see the end of the world. Domenico Laffi, in 1673, called the trip a whim. If you are not sure why you are going, you are in old company.
The old rites, without the fire

The Concello de Fisterra names two. The first is the bath: the pilgrim washed off the dust of the road at the beach of Langosteira, two kilometres before the village, and began the last approach clean. The second is the sunset, which the Concello calls death and resurrection: the sun dying in the sea, and rising the next day, as the pilgrim rises in the daily walking. You do not have to believe in any of it. You can take the first as a way of washing, and the second as an hour to be quiet.

Muxía has its own old gesture. On the Camiño da Pel, the "Way of the Skin", pilgrims washed at a fountain before they entered the sanctuary. The fountain is gone, the Xunta says, but its name is still on the path.
Walking with a question
You do not need a question, but if you have one it will keep you company. Here is one for each day, to take or leave.

items.t: Santiago to Negreira.
You have just arrived somewhere. What did it finish for you, and what did it leave open?
Negreira to Olveiroa.
This is the long day. What do you carry that you could set down?
Olveiroa to Corcubión.
You see the sea at last, far off. What are you walking towards?
Corcubión to Fisterra.
What would you like to leave behind that cannot be burned?
Fisterra to Muxía.
After the end of the earth, what comes next, and what does the road ask of you on the way back to a life?

spans.t: For every kind of walker

If you walk with faith, the sanctuary at Muxía and the church of Santa María das Areas at Fisterra are places for quiet. If you do not, they are quiet and cool, and worth a rest. If your reason is grief, give yourself leave to feel it at the edge of the sea. If you walk to get fit, let the beauty in anyway. The road does not ask you for a reason at the door. It asks you to keep walking, and then to stand still and look at the sea.
What this walk is not

Start with what the official pages do not say. The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago issues the Compostela to those who come to the tomb of the Apostle for religious and/or spiritual reasons and follow the routes of the Way on foot, by bicycle or on horseback. On foot or on horseback, the Office asks for at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that it recognises, and says that the final stage must include at least the last one leading into the Cathedral. Your credencial, stamped along the way, is the proof. That is a walk that arrives at Santiago. This one begins there, and leaves.

The Office's pages read for this book say nothing about Fisterra or Muxía. This book therefore says nothing about what the Office does or does not record for this walk. If you want to know whether it would note your journey, in any form, ask it directly.
The Fisterrana
The town of Fisterra has its own certificate. The Concello de Fisterra, the town council, writes on its page for the end of the Way that the
Fisterrana

is an official certification obtained at the municipal pilgrims' hostel and at the tourist office, certifying that you have reached "the end of the world". The route you have walked is shown by your credencial, with its stamps or signatures from parishes, hostels and other places on the road. For groups of more than ten people, the council asks you to contact the tourist office or the hostel first. The page gives no opening hours, and this book names none. Ask when you arrive, and have your credencial in your hand.
The Muxiana
Muxía has its own as well, the
Muxiana

. Two official sources place it at the tourist office. The Xunta's stage text for the road into Muxía says that the Muxiana can be obtained at the tourist office, calls it an end-of-Camino credential, and adds that Fisterra provides the equivalent, the Fisterrana, which can be stamped at the municipal hostel. Spain's official tourism website says the same, and calls the Muxiana the Muxía pilgrim's certificate. No page read for this book says whether you need to have walked from Santiago, in which order you must take the two capes, or how many stamps you need. Ask at the tourist office.
At the cape, and at Muxía

The cape is not the town: the Xunta's stage ends at the lighthouse, which it calls kilometre zero, and the way up leads past the church of Santa María das Areas. Give yourself the evening, and if you can, the next morning in no hurry. At Muxía, the Concello says that arriving at the sanctuary is the expected reward for the effort of reaching the end of the Way. Walk round the stones slowly. Many people simply stand and look.
The way back

Do not leave getting back to chance. The Xunta's bus site, bus.gal, is where to look for the times of public buses, and your hostel or the tourist office can tell you what runs this week. Do not plan a flight or a train home for the afternoon of your last walking day. If you have a day to spare, spend it by the sea. The walk will be over soon enough.
A short walk ends quickly, and ordinary life returns faster than the walk leaves you. Do not try to settle it all at once.

Keep three things. Keep the credencial and any certificate you collected. Keep the page you wrote on the cape, if you wrote one, and read it again in a month. Keep the walk itself in a small form: twenty minutes on foot each day, without a phone, is enough to remember what the road asked of you.

Do not worry if you cannot explain it. The sea is hard to describe to someone who was not there, and the shorter the walk, the harder it is to say what it changed. Say one thing you saw, and let that be enough.

The Pilgrim's Office, on its page for after the pilgrimage, offers two thoughts. Some pilgrims, it says, would like to give back to the Way as much as they received, perhaps as hosts at a hostel. And if you wish to continue the spiritual journey you began, it suggests that you may talk to your parish priest, or join a local association of St James.
If you walk again, a road that ends in Santiago is waiting. It may look different now that you have walked from the cathedral to the sea.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus
. The app is still in development, so look in it for what is available on the road to Finisterre and Muxía today, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures, bus times and weather.
A reminder about the passport: the sources in this book ask for the stamped paper credencial. A passport in any app is a keepsake until an official source says otherwise.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and the fact ledger that goes with it lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: The Xunta de Galicia

(caminodesantiago.gal): the Fisterra and Muxía Way, its stage pages and their lengths, the advice for walkers, and its news archive. Also a 2013 heritage report on the old roads of Santiago, on a Xunta site, for the history of the road.
The Concello de Fisterra
, the town council, and its pages on the end of the Way: the stages, the rites and the Fisterrana.
The Concello de Muxía
(concellomuxia.com): the sanctuary, the stones, the history of the town and the route from Santiago.
Turismo de Galicia
, the regional tourism board: the cape and the sanctuary.
Spain's official tourism website
(spain.info): the route's five stages and the Muxiana.
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
(oficinadelperegrino.com): the rules of the Compostela, the credencial, the pilgrimage's history and the page on life after it.
AEMET
and
MeteoGalicia
, the Spanish and Galician weather services, as places to look for a forecast.
Wikipedia

, for history and geography: the articles on Cape Finisterre, Fisterra, Muxía, the Costa da Morte, the Camino de Santiago, Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus, the Jacobean Holy Year, Santiago airport and Galicia, and, in Spanish, the Finisterre lighthouse. The 1991 to 2020 figures for Santiago are Wikipedia's, from AEMET.
Galicia Press, El Debate and Vive Camino
, for what has been reported about the custom of burning boots, and one travel agency's route page, as a second view of the stages. Each is named where it is used.
A standard solar calculation
, for sunrise and sunset at the cape.
The CaminoPlus route catalog
, for the road's name, ends and ~90 km. The catalog gives no stage count.

spans.t: Published lengths differ, sometimes by a few kilometres, and this book says so. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.

Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: the associations of friends of the Camino, the hosts who open the hostels, the councils and volunteers who keep the paths and the cape clean, and the people in the towns and villages who point the way and say
Buen Camino
to a stranger.
A short glossary

items.t: Albergue
: a pilgrims' hostel with shared rooms.
Buen Camino
: "good Way", the greeting between pilgrims.
Camiño
: Galician for a path or way.
Concello
: a Galician town council.
Credencial
: the pilgrim's passport.
Cruceiro
: a Galician stone cross.
Fisterrana
and
Muxiana
: the certificates of Fisterra and Muxía.
Hórreo
: a granary on stone legs.
Hospitalero
: the host of a pilgrims' hostel.
Menú del peregrino
: a set meal for pilgrims.
Pazo
: a Galician manor house.
Ría
: a long sea inlet.
Sello
: a stamp in the credencial.
Xunta
: the regional government of Galicia.
